subject: RNG functions in models - design issues

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: RNG functions in models - design issues
parts:
We want to be able to have random number generating
functions accessible through the models. I see
them being used in the following blocks for the following
purposes (please help me fill in things I've missed here):

block: transformed data
use: random data generation
issue: only way to save is with generated quantity
variable set to value

block: transformed parameters
use: random parameters
issues: transformed param block executes before model;
inefficient to assign double values to agrad::var

block: model
use: random intermediate quantities
issues: no way to save (can use transformed params to save)

block: generated quantities
use: forward sampling
issues: none

There are three relevant blocks in the generated code for the model:

constructor() reading data and transforming data
log_prob() computation
write_csv() transforming params and generating the generated quantities

The model doesn't hold a reference to the random number generator
used by the sampler -- the sampler does. In this case, the hmc_base
base class holds the random number generators. The samplers then call
the constructor once to create the model, including reading data and
generating transformed data. The log_prob() function is called repeatedly
during the leapfrog iterations. The write_csv() function is called
once per iteration to do the write.

This just seems odd to me -- having both non-deterministic data
and a non-deterministic log prob. The non-deterministic log prob
means successive calls to log_prob with RNGs in different states
can produce different answers. That's only possible if we allow
randomization in transformed parameters.

So the sampler would have to pass in an RNG to these functions
as an argument. We can't put the RNG in the model itself, because
the model's set up to be called concurrently from multiple threads,
but RNGs aren't thread safe. (The L'Ecuyer setup uses different
samplers in different threads that are initialized to be independent.)

A remaining issue is whether to specify the RNG argument as a reference
or as a pointer. Pointers give us the option of passing 0 in the
case the log prob function doesn't need an RNG. On the other hand,
simple Boost RNGs are very cheap to construct from a simple seed
and you only need to do it once, so I'm inclined to go with a reference.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RNG functions in models - design issues
parts:
I'd add a new block as a future use case for the random number generation capability.

block: parameter initialization
use: random initialization of parameters, potentially based on data
issues: none that I can see

This is highly relevant for time-series models where, given the parameters of a time series, it makes no sense to sample the state variables of the time series independently.

Anything which makes log_prob() non-deterministic seems like trouble to me and probably should be avoided.  What's the real use case for sampling in the transformed parameters?  I can't think of a valid use for this.  I can see the use for randomly perturbed (or generated) data, but I'm not certain it's necessary as most people using Stan will be getting their data from other environments (eg, R, Matlab, etc) which can happily synthesize data.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RNG functions in models - design issues
parts:
On 8/15/12 4:21 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> I'd add a new block as a future use case for the random number generation capability.
>
> block: parameter initialization
> use: random initialization of parameters, potentially based on data
> issues: none that I can see

That's a great idea, and I think we should do it.
All the code's already in place to test the bounds
and do the transforms.

We probably want to somehow test that all the parameters
got initialized this way, or provide some way to
auto-initialize the others.

> This is highly relevant for time-series models where, given the parameters of a time series, it makes no sense to sample
> the state variables of the time series independently.
>
> Anything which makes log_prob() non-deterministic seems like trouble to me and probably should be avoided. What's the
> real use case for sampling in the transformed parameters? I can't think of a valid use for this.

I was thinking random latent variables that weren't recorded.
Things like making a choice of latent mixture component.
That seems like weak justification at best, though, and
couldn't really be communicated to other parameters.

I also can't think of another case where you might want
to generate a random quantity based on the value of a parameter.

> I can see the use for
> randomly perturbed (or generated) data, but I'm not certain it's necessary as most people using Stan will be getting
> their data from other environments (eg, R, Matlab, etc) which can happily synthesize data.

Andrew made the point that we don't want to have to
write the same model multiple times. On the other hand,
I don't see how to avoid that, even if we can put it all
in Stan, because the generated quantities block would look
different.

The main use is motivated by Andrew's desire to do what
he calls "forward sampling", meaning generating fake data
based on fitted parameters. That will all go in the
generated quantities block, though, and again, there are
no issues there I can see.

If we restrict random functions to transformed data and
generated quantities (plus future inits), then we can overload
sampling notation for them w/o ambiguity. That is, write

x ~ normal(0,1);

to assign x to a random unit normal variate instead of

x <- normal_random(0,1);

- Bob

That's the only way I see how to do it.

1. Random inits on the unbounded representation
2. (inverse) transform to the natural scales,
3. user init code overrides vars on natural scales,
4. constraint check on natural scales
5. transform back to unconstrained representation.

The efficiency concern of some extra transforms are nothing
here because the same transforms are done every leapfrog step!

> That seems like weak justification at best, though, and
> couldn't really be communicated to other parameters.
>
>
> Wouldn't the choice of a latent mixture component be marginalized out or explicitly parameterized?

Probably. It's unlikely you'd make it and want
to forget it. So this motivation's a stretch at best.

> I also can't think of another case where you might want
> to generate a random quantity based on the value of a parameter.
>
>
> > I can see the use for
>

> in Stan, because the generated quantities block would look
> different.
>
>
> I'm not sure how that would require writting the same model multiple times though. The data would change, but the model
> itself would remain the same, right?

The problem is that you write matching sampling
statements both in the model and in the generated quantities,
as in:

model {
...
y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
...
}
generated quantities {
...
y_rep <- normal_random(mu,sigma);
...
}

If we replaced the generated quantities notation with sampling
notation, that'd just be

generated quantities {
...
y_rep ~ normal(mu,sigma);
...

}

>
>
> The main use is motivated by Andrew's desire to do what
> he calls "forward sampling", meaning generating fake data
> based on fitted parameters. That will all go in the
> generated quantities block, though, and again, there are
> no issues there I can see.
>
>
> The forward sampling case makes sense to me. It could be done with stan right now without using a generated quantities
> block, but it wouldn't be as statistically efficient.

Exactly. That's why the generated quantities block
was added. Instead of using MCMC a la HMC/NUTS with all its
gradient complexity and multiple leapfrog steps, we'd
just be doing plain old MC sampling given a parameter and
its variables, at least in the usual graphical model case.

>
>
> If we restrict random functions to transformed data and
> generated quantities (plus future inits), then we can overload
> sampling notation for them w/o ambiguity. That is, write
>
> x ~ normal(0,1);
>
> to assign x to a random unit normal variate instead of
>
> x <- normal_random(0,1);
>
>
>
> Agreed. I also like ~ much more myself.

As long as nobody else makes a good argument against it,
I'll try that and see how it looks.

Thanks for all the great feedback and suggestions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RNG functions in models - design issues
parts:
The C preprocessor is completely distinct from the rest of the compiler and can be used separately to use #include, #define, #if, etc.  In fact, you can do this already with a script.  For instance:

cpp -I<incdir> model-withmacros.stan model.stan
stanc model.stan
...

The call to cpp could be done directly in stanc if we wanted to support that functionality directly but you can also just call it yourself.

Cheers,
Marcus

We could write our own little preprocessor
for #include. We could also use C's as Marcus
suggests, which would give us that for free.
The biggest issue is dealing with things like line
numbers in error output. The parser's taking
in a string iterator with line number tracking, and
it's not sophisticated enough to know it's in a
subfile. We'd have to do something like translate
the error outputs.

I'm very anti-macro, though, as it makes things
very hard to debug, even if we get line numbers right.

I'd rather introduce simple macro-like function
definitions. If we have syntax that's context dependent,
the issue is whether we could reuse it or not.

- Bob

Another way to solve the problem is to make it (relatively) easy to define complicated new model classes.  For example, suppose that I start using the varying-intercepts, varying-slopes model all over the place and I'd like to "macro" it.  Then I could create a new model class that expresses this model as a function of its list of parameters.  Creating a model class is more effort than writing a macro but it could be worth it for models that are used over and over again.
A

I knew it was possible, but didn't realize it
was this easy -- the C++ compilers let
you see all sorts of intermediate stages of the
work they do.

I'm very tempted NOT to mention this in manuals,
etc., and leave it to the C whizzes to do on their

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RNG functions in models - design issues
parts: On Thu, Aug 16, 2012 at 4:59 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On 8/16/12 11:33 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
The C preprocessor is completely distinct from the rest of the compiler and can be used separately to use #include,
#define, #if, etc.  In fact, you can do this already with a script.  For instance:

cpp -I<incdir> model-withmacros.stan model.stan
stanc model.stan
...

The call to cpp could be done directly in stanc if we wanted to support that functionality directly but you can also
just call it yourself.

I knew it was possible, but didn't realize it
was this easy -- the C++ compilers let
you see all sorts of intermediate stages of the
work they do.

I'm very tempted NOT to mention this in manuals,
etc., and leave it to the C whizzes to do on their
own.  The only issue is that then their models
wouldn't work in the in the R interface.  (Maybe
we could put an expert mode expand macros in or
something.)

The brute force approach is to call cpp with a system call from the parser to produce a temp file which gets parsed per usual.  More sophisticated (although perhaps more work?) is to use something like Wave (http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_50_0/libs/wave/index.html).  I'm not sure how it fits into the existing parser framework, but given that it's part of boost, it may work well.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: won't work: Boost Wave as standalone macro preprocessor
parts:
Looks like we can't use Boost Wave as a standalone
preprocessor because it's tied into the C lexer.

Here's a query to the Boost Spirit mailing list and a reply from
Hartmut Kaiser, the developer:

> Yes the use case is Use wave as **only** for preprocessing ...
> I need to iterate characters and some direction on writing the NEW
> iterator.

Sorry that does not work. You can't use Wave for preprocessing only. It is
built on top of a tokenizer (lexer) and operates itself with tokens.

- Bob
